evidence.text: A burning candle; the rays of the sun
Origin unclear. Used in ancient texts to mean "white" and "hundred" (百).
西方色也。陰用事，物色白。从入合二。二，陰數。凡白之屬皆从白。

Unclear; probably a pictogram (象形).
Guo (1954) suggests that it represents a thumb and is original form of 拇 (*mɯʔ) or, more probably, 擘 (*preːɡ).
Alternatively, Unger (apud Schuessler, 2007) suggests that it represents an acorn, noting its use in 樂 /乐 (“oak”) (= 櫟 /栎) and 皂 (zào, “acorn”). In this interpretation, the meaning of “white” is derived from the color of an acorn's inside. Unrelated to the top component of 原.
STEDT derives it from Proto-Sino-Tibetan *bawk (“white”), whence also Proto-Bodo-Garo *bok (“white”), Limbu ᤑ (phô, “white”); also compare Proto-Mon-Khmer *kɓɔɔk (“white, grey”).
However, Schuessler (2007) finds it difficult to reconcile these forms with Middle Chinese due to the lack of medial r. Instead, he proposes a derivation from Proto-Sino-Tibetan *bar (“white”) with -k extension, thus cognate with 皤 (OC *baːl, “white”) (Wang, 1982), Mizo vâr (“(to be) white”), Proto-Karen *ʔ(b)wa (“white”).

white; pure, unblemished; bright

evidence.source: 王寧, “再說『白』字之本義,” 復旦大學出土文獻與古文字研究中心
evidence.text: The author reports that oracle-bone 白 was used for the color word 白, the title 伯, and a place name. He surveys proposals that the graph depicts cloth, a thumb, flame/light, a face or head, or a vessel, and rejects the thumb and head arguments as unproven. He then argues that 白 depicts an ancient cooking/measuring vessel 鬴/釜, with its middle stroke representing the joined lid and vessel; this is the author's own hypothesis, not an established consensus. He cautions that archaeological identification of an uninscribed vessel cannot establish what it was called in Shang times.
evidence.title: 王寧：再說“白”字之本義

evidence.source: 王寧, “再說『白』字之本義,” 復旦大學出土文獻與古文字研究中心
evidence.text: The article says oracle-bone examples use 白 for “white,” 伯, and a place name. Its author treats the white-color and lord/elder uses as phonetic loans, but the article also presents rival accounts of the graph's original referent. No dated individual inscription or securely reconstructed pronunciation of a depicted vessel is established on this page; the proposal therefore does not independently establish that vessel's name or sound.
evidence.title: 王寧：再說“白”字之本義

evidence.text: The entry presents oracle-bone, Western Zhou bronze, Warring States, seal, clerical and regular-script forms. It interprets the oracle-bone shape as a thumb with a fingerprint and says bronze and Warring States forms continue it; it describes the small-seal upper short stroke as arising from brush movement and the clerical/regular forms as increasingly obscuring the proposed original shape. This thumb reading is one account among disputed proposals, not independently verified here.
evidence.title: 白字形演变字源_汉字「白」

evidence.text: The page labels the charted forms Shang, Western Zhou, Shuowen/small seal, and Ming; it reports Mandarin bái (also bó) and gives competing comparative etymologies: STEDT's Proto-Sino-Tibetan *bawk analysis and Schuessler's alternative *bar with a -k extension, citing a medial-r mismatch in reconciling the former with Middle Chinese. These are word-etymology proposals, not accounts of graphic components. No sound component is proposed for 白 itself.

The author rejects thumb and face/head arguments as insufficiently evidenced and proposes a cooking or measuring vessel 鬴/釜, with the middle stroke marking the seam between vessel and lid. This is the author's hypothesis, not a consensus.

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, 小學堂每日一字
evidence.text: This educational database identifies 白 as a thumb pictograph and proposes that the thumb's position as the leading digit motivates 伯 (eldest/leader). It says 白 was often written for 伯 in oracle-bone texts and was later borrowed for the color word, with 人 added to 伯 to distinguish it. This differs from Wang Ning's analysis and remains a source-specific interpretation.
evidence.title: 每日一字

evidence.text: The entry records Mandarin Standard Chinese bái and a restricted literary bó, and Cantonese Guangzhou/Hong Kong Jyutping baak6. It gives Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *bˤrak and Zhengzhang *braːɡ for 白. It summarizes competing word-history proposals: STEDT's Proto-Sino-Tibetan *bawk and Schuessler's alternative *bar with a -k extension, with the latter motivated by difficulty matching the former's lack of medial r to Middle Chinese. These are lexical etymologies, not component analyses of the graph.

editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

gaps: No accessible source in this research established a consensus account of the original depicted object; thumb, cloth, light/flame, head/face, vessel, and other proposals remain disputed. The cited Fudan article advances the vessel hypothesis but explicitly notes the naming problem for archaeological objects.

The supplied Shuowen text gives Xu Shen's Han-era analysis (“from 入 joined with 二; 二 is the yin number”) and color definition, but this research did not inspect a primary Shuowen page or verify it against excavated early forms; treat it as a historical explanation, not confirmation of graphic origin.

The Fudan article reports oracle-bone uses for white, 伯, and a place name, but this research did not retrieve individually dated inscription contexts or establish when each semantic use began. Exact earliest attestation dates for the color sense, 伯/elder/title, and place-name use remain unresolved.

百 appears in the supplied dossier as an ancient use, but external pages inspected here did not establish its earliest attestation or a secure semantic link to 白. No chronology should be inferred from the order of glosses.
The source packet's candle/sun-rays explanation and its acorn hypothesis were not independently corroborated by the inspected primary or scholarly pages. They remain unsupported here.

Modern readings in the dossier were not independently checked across reference works. Wiktionary's opened page confirms Mandarin bái and also lists bó; historical phonological reconstructions in the dossier belong to different systems and cannot by themselves establish a depicted object's name.
The CUHK database result appeared in search results to describe a thumb and loan to the color word, but its page timed out when opened, so that claim is not counted as inspected evidence.

The Fudan article's reported oracle-bone uses are not accompanied by individually dated inscription contexts on the inspected page; earliest attestation dates and sense order for white, 伯, and the place name remain unresolved.
The original referent is unsettled: the thumb account is presented by Academia Sinica, while the 2010 Fudan author rejects it and proposes a vessel. Neither account is demonstrated as consensus.
No independent evidence establishes the ancient name or pronunciation of the proposed vessel. A reconstructed pronunciation of the word 白 cannot establish the name of a depicted object.

The Fudan author proposes a sound/borrowing relation between 白 and 伯 but does not supply a dated phonological argument on the inspected page. The Academia Sinica account offers a semantic thumb-to-eldest explanation instead; the link remains disputed.

The relationship of 百 to 白 is contested in the inspected Fudan article, which proposes a vessel-content interpretation for 百. This research did not establish an earliest dated 百 attestation or a secure semantic development from white.
The Shuowen wording in the dossier remains a Han-era historical explanation; no Shuowen source page was inspected in this invocation to verify its text or compare it directly with excavated forms.

The proposed glyph files are modern vector redrawings. No image pixels or underlying archaeological inscription were visually inspected here; captions should be read as script-style candidates, not as verified facsimiles of particular artifacts.
The opened reconstruction and lexical reference pages do not resolve the graphic origin, and no sound component is proposed for 白.

Earlier guessed upload paths recorded in the supplied acquisition findings were not reused. The exact links exposed by the source pages differ.

The sources disagree on the graph’s original referent and on the direction of the relationship between the 伯 and color uses: Academia Sinica gives 白 → 伯 by semantic development from a thumb and later borrowing for color; Wang Ning treats both 伯 and color 白 as loans from a proposed vessel graph. The inspected sources do not settle this direction, so the directed development from color 白 to 伯 should be removed or represented as unresolved.

The reports of oracle-bone uses do not establish which sense was first: no individual inscription contexts with independently verified dates were inspected. CUHK supplies corpus identifiers, but this research did not verify those inscriptions against primary facsimiles or dating records.
No independently established ancient vessel name or pronunciation supports Wang Ning’s vessel proposal. A reconstruction of 白 itself cannot establish the name or sound of the depicted object.

The CUHK page describes 白 as borrowed for the numeral 百 and provides oracle-bone examples, while Wang Ning proposes a different vessel/content account for 百. This research does not establish a secure semantic link or earliest dated 百 use.
The competing source accounts do not alter the supplied glyph selections: this research did not inspect the glyph images or find evidence requiring a caption or selection correction.
